title: Bottleneck-Guided Spectral Subgoals For Offline Goal-Conditioned RL
one_liner: Long-horizon offline navigation is like crossing a mountain range: find the actual passes and send the robot through them, not by time or luck.
lead: An offline robot or agent learns to reach any goal from old recorded data, but the hardest part is finding paths through choke points (narrow passages where the goal is only reachable one way). Most methods pick intermediate waypoints by counting steps or by a shallow guess. This paper finds the actual choke points in the offline data using a clustering math trick, then forces the high-level planner to route through them, turning a chaotic long-horizon puzzle into a chain of short simple steps.

problem.h2: Long-horizon offline navigation is chaotic without structure
paras: An offline agent learns to reach any goal from a fixed dataset of recorded trajectories (no live interaction). On tasks that take many steps, the agent must chain together dozens of moves without exploration or correction. The naive approach: train the agent to copy the dataset, then at test time ask it to reach a new goal it has never seen. This breaks because the agent has no map of which intermediate states are necessary stops on the way.

Most prior hierarchical methods pick waypoints (intermediate targets) using time-based rules (every N steps) or by short-horizon value heuristics (is this state worth a small reward in 1-2 steps?). These miss the true structure: the offline data shows some state regions are tightly linked (many trajectories bounce between them) while others are loosely linked (few paths cross between them). Certain narrow regions act as unavoidable passages — the robot can only reach the goal by passing through them. Without explicit knowledge of these passages, the agent makes bad high-level decisions and gets stuck.

callout.html: Find the actual bottlenecks in offline data using spectral math, then force navigation plans through them.

steps.text: Use spectral clustering math on the offline dataset to find state-space regions that are weakly connected.
Identify states that lie on the boundary between clusters (these are the natural passages).
Select the most typical boundary states as mandatory waypoints, then build a graph of which keypoint can reach which.

steps.text: Train the high-level planner to pick only these keypoints as subgoals, never arbitrary states.

object.h2: What the paper changes: subgoal selection
paras: Most hierarchical methods treat the choice of subgoals (intermediate targets) as an independent problem: pick them by a heuristic, then train a low-level policy to reach them. This paper binds subgoal selection to the data's connection patterns. It chooses subgoals by asking: where in the offline data are the narrow passages where trajectories must funnel through? The change is algorithmic: instead of time-step sampling or value-based filtering, it uses spectral clustering to find which state regions are loosely connected and restricts subgoals to boundary states.

hidden.name: Degree of structural separation
paras: The paper uncovers a hidden quantity called the bottleneck, inferred from the Laplacian eigenvector of the state-space graph. A bottleneck is a state where many diverse offline trajectories are forced to pass through on their way to different goals. Mathematically, it is a region with low probability of transitioning directly to distant target regions, making it a necessary intermediate step. The Laplacian eigenvalues quantify this: large gaps in the eigenvector signal strong bottlenecks; smooth transitions signal open regions.

The paper estimates this by building a graph of state transitions from the offline dataset, computing its Laplacian matrix (a standard linear-algebra tool), and examining the second-smallest eigenvector. States where this eigenvector changes abruptly are boundary regions; states where it clusters with many dataset neighbors are strong bottlenecks.

heat.caption: Darker and highlighted show stronger bottleneck (more trajectories must pass through).

reads.html: A bottleneck is a state that nearly all successful paths must visit. Finding it means looking at which states separate the offline data into independent regions.
Laplacian spectral clustering partitions the state graph into clusters (regions), and boundary states between clusters are bottlenecks (metastable sets in the paper's language).

mechanism.h2: Why it works: structure guides planning
paras: The core insight is that offline data is not random. It has patterns: some state regions are tightly connected (trajectories easily go back and forth), other regions are weakly connected (paths must traverse a narrow gate). A high-level planner that ignores this structure wastes time and fails — it asks for impossible transitions. But a high-level planner that is forced to respect the bottlenecks makes decisions that the low-level controller can actually execute because the offline data shows evidence that paths between bottlenecks exist.

Spectral clustering finds this structure automatically. The Laplacian matrix of the state-transition graph has a natural spectral property: its smallest eigenvector splits the graph into clusters, and the transition costs between clusters are minimized exactly at the bottlenecks. So when the high-level plan only chooses subgoals at bottleneck states, it is choosing stepping stones that the offline data proves are reachable from one another. The low-level controller then only needs to learn short hops, which is easier and more reliable than long, chaotic long-horizon leaps, because the low-level problem has fewer steps, so the controller has fewer chances to accumulate errors and more examples in the data of how to bridge each pair of keypoints.

Theoretically, under a property called metastable decomposition (the state space naturally decomposes into a few loosely-coupled regions), routing through bottlenecks yields a subgoal structure that is provably near-optimal in terms of hitting time — the expected steps to reach the goal. In practice (measured from real experiments on benchmark tasks), this translates to higher success rates on long-horizon tasks because the agent never makes an impossible high-level request.

stages.s: Partition into clusters and identify boundaries
Select boundary states as keypoints and build reachability graph
Train high-level planner restricted to keypoints
Hierarchical policy: high-level picks keypoint subgoals, low-level executes transitions

math.h2: The equation: finding bottlenecks via the Laplacian
math.words: Partition the state-transition graph to minimize the edge crossing cost; the bottleneck states are those that lie on the boundary of the partition with minimum crossing penalty.
math.equation: L_graph = D - A, where L is the Laplacian, D is degree matrix, A is adjacency. Eigenvector v2 (second-smallest) partitions: clusters = sign(v2). Bottleneck states = argmax_s |gradient of v2 at s|.
symbols: Diagonal matrix; D_ii = how many transitions from state i
Adjacency matrix; A_ij = 1 if data contains transition i to j
Second-smallest eigenvector of L (separates graph into two clusters)
State where eigenvector value changes most steeply across the graph

worked.title: Tiny worked example
lines: Imagine 6 states in offline data. States 1-3 transition freely among themselves (open region). States 4-6 do likewise. Only trajectories have moves from state 3 to state 4 (the gate).
Adjacency A captures this: A_33 = 2, A_34 = 2, A_43 = 2, A_44 = 2. Other inter-region entries = 0.
Degree D: states 1,2 have degree 2 each (local). States 3,4 have degree 4 each (connected to both regions). States 5,6 have degree 2.
Laplacian L = D - A. The second eigenvector v2 will be negative in region 1-3, positive in region 4-6, and change value most steeply (largest rate of change) at state 3 and state 4.
These two states are the bottleneck. The algorithm selects them as keypoints. Any high-level plan must route through (3 or 4).

math.note: The Laplacian eigenvector acts like a hidden topographic map; the steepest slopes reveal the passes.

items.b: Dataset is too sparse or random.
items.html: If the offline data does not actually visit the bottlenecks (for instance, the data is noise or only covers one task), spectral clustering will not find clear cluster boundaries, and the method fails silently — the discovered keypoints are irrelevant.

The theory assumes the state space naturally decomposes into a few semi-independent regions. If the world is a continuous blob (all states mix freely), there are no true bottlenecks, and forcing waypoints through arbitrary boundaries wastes steps.

If the offline data never demonstrates a path from one discovered keypoint to another, the reachability graph will have gaps, and the high-level planner will request impossible transitions that the low-level controller cannot fulfill.

The data is rich, covers the bottleneck states densely, and the environment truly has a few critical passages (mazes, multi-room navigation, pick-and-place with articulated steps). The method then improves success rate substantially because the high-level planner no longer wastes computation on impossible transitions and the low-level controller can focus on well-evidenced short transitions that appear many times in the offline data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small test: an offline dataset of trajectories in a multi-room maze (2-3 rooms, each connected via a hallway). Train a standard offline RL agent on all trajectories (baseline). Train a spectral-bottleneck agent on the same data. Then ask both agents to reach a new goal in a room they have visited but via a path they have never taken. Measure: (1) success rate (did the agent reach the goal?), (2) average episode length (how many steps did it take?), (3) planning time (how much wall-clock time for high-level and low-level decisions?).
demo.metric_eq: Success = (goals_reached / total_goals_attempted). Episode_length = total_steps_per_episode. Planning_time = high_level_latency + low_level_latency.
demo.closing: The spectral-bottleneck agent should reach goals reliably in fewer steps because it respects the maze structure; the baseline should fail or wander because it has no map of the passages.
